title: The lions that faced the wrong way
translation: In Tanba there's a place called Izumo, with a fine shrine they built by bringing over the god of the great Izumo Shrine. The land belonged to a man called Shida-something, and one autumn he invited the priest Shōkai and a whole group of others: "Come on, let's go to Izumo and pray. I'll treat you to rice cakes." So they all went, said their prayers, and felt very devout.

The guardian lions in front of the shrine were standing back to front. Shōkai was deeply moved. "Oh, how wonderful! I've never seen the lions placed like this. There must be some deep meaning to it." His eyes filled with tears. "Come on, don't any of you see how special this is? Honestly!"

Now everyone was amazed. "It really is like nowhere else. We have to tell them about this back home." But Shōkai wanted to know more. He called over one of the shrine staff, an older man who looked like he'd know. "The way the lions here are placed must surely follow some tradition. I'd love to hear about it."
"Oh, that," the man said. "Some naughty children did that. Outrageous." He walked over, turned them back the right way, and left. So Shōkai's tears were for nothing.

literal: In Tanba there is a place called Izumo.
They transferred (the spirit of) the great shrine and built it splendidly.

Since it was a place governed by someone called Shida-something, around autumn he invited Holy Man Shōkai and many other people too, (saying) 'Come now, to worship at Izumo. I will have you eat kaimochi', and took them along; each of them worshipped and felt great faith.

The lion and guardian dog in front (of the shrine) were standing turned away, facing backward, so the holy man was greatly moved: 'Ah, how splendid! The way these lions stand is very unusual. There must be a deep reason', he said with tears in his eyes, 'Well, gentlemen, do you not notice this remarkable thing? That is too bad of you.' When he said this,
each of them wondered at it: 'Truly it is different from others; let's tell of it as a souvenir for the capital', they said, and

the holy man, wanting to know still more, called a shrine official whose face looked mature and as if he surely knew things: 'The way the lions of this shrine have been placed: surely there is some tradition to it. I would like to hear a little.' When he said this,
'About that: mischievous children did it; it is outrageous', (the official) said,
went up close, set them straight and left, so the holy man's tears of emotion came to nothing.

notes.quote: 丹波に出雲といふ所あり
notes.text: Not the famous Izumo Shrine in Izumo province, but a shrine with the same name in Tanba, west of Kyoto. It is usually identified with today's Izumo Daijingū in Kameoka.

The host gets his guests to come with food. かいもちひ is some kind of rice cake or dumpling; scholars do not agree on the exact dish. {召|め}させむ: {召|め}さ, from {召|め}す 'to eat' (respectful), + せ, from す 'have someone do', + む 'I will'.

A pair of guardian figures in front of a shrine: a lion ({獅子|しし}) and a 'Korean dog' ({狛犬|こまいぬ}). In Kenkō's time they were probably small wooden figures directly in front of the sanctuary, not the big stone pairs at the gate that you see today. That is why the official can simply walk over and turn them round. They normally face outward, toward the people who come, to guard the shrine. These two had turned their backs on the visitors.
む: a guess, 'there must be'. This is Kenkō's target: the man who finds deep meaning everywhere before he asks a simple question.
{無下|むげ}: 'terrible, beneath contempt'. Shōkai scolds the others for not being moved. A minute later they are all moved.

notes.quote: おとなしく物知りぬべき顔したる
notes.text: おとなし is a false friend: 'mature, sensible', not modern 'quiet'. ぬべき: 'surely'. The official looks like an expert, and he is one, about one simple fact.

notes.quote: さがなき童どもの仕りける
notes.text: さがなし: 'mischievous, naughty'. After Shōkai's long, polite and moved speech, the answer comes in two flat sentences. The official speaks in polite {候|さうらふ} style, which makes it even drier.

notes.quote: 感涙いたづらになりにけり
notes.text: いたづら: 'useless, in vain'. In modern Japanese, いたずら means 'a prank', and the tears were caused by a prank. That double meaning is an accident of later language history, but it fits too well to leave out. (The old meaning also survives: modern いたずらに means 'in vain'.)
